books.section: Topic 5.8 Military Conflict in the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1861. Public domain; quoted as printed in Barron’s, Chapter 7.
stimulus.text:
“I have no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the States where it exists. I believe I have no lawful right to do so, and I have no inclination to do so.”

—Abraham Lincoln, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1861

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: In this passage, Lincoln promises that he will

options.text: not interfere with slavery where it already existed.
abolish slavery in every state at once.
options.misconception: Lincoln promises the opposite: he says he will not interfere where slavery exists.

options.text: extend slavery into the western territories.
options.misconception: Lincoln says nothing here about extending slavery. Background: his party opposed its extension.

options.text: allow the Southern states to secede in peace.
options.misconception: Lincoln promises not to touch slavery where it exists, not to accept secession.

rationales.A: Lincoln says plainly he has no purpose to interfere with slavery in the states where it exists.
rationales.B: Lincoln promises the opposite: he says he will not interfere where slavery exists.
rationales.C: Lincoln says nothing here about extending slavery. Background: his party opposed its extension.
rationales.D: Lincoln promises not to touch slavery where it exists, not to accept secession.
rationales.general:
1. Lincoln names the institution directly: slavery, in the states where it exists.
2. He denies both the purpose and the right to interfere with it there.
3. He adds that he has no inclination to do so, closing the door twice over.
4. The promise is narrow on purpose: it covers slavery where it already exists, nothing more.
Remember: read the promise’s limits: where it exists is the whole of it.
